full_judgment:
Mr. A.B.M. Khairul Haque J:  This Rule Nisi was issued at the instance of Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation, calling upon the Chairman, second Labour court. Dhaka and another to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 26.4.2001 passed by the Second Labour Court, Dhaka in 1.R.0 case No. 26 of 1994 (Annexure-C) should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 

 2. The facts as stated in the petition, in brief, are that Jinnatul Hossain, the respondent No. 2, was in employee under the Bangladesh Agricultural Corporation Development (BADC). Her filed a Labour Case being I.R.O Case No. 26 of 1994 before the Second Labour Court, Dhaka under Section 34 of the Industrial Relation Ordinance, 1969 (IRO in Short) against the Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation (BADC in short) and others praying for emoluments for the period from 1.6.1976 to 12.12.1988 with bonus etc. and also for compensation. The said case was contested on behalf of the petitioner. 

 3. After hearing the labour Court by its judgment and order dated 26.4.2001, allowed the case on contest in part, directing the BADC to pay wages during the period of suspension of the petitioner excluding the amount paid as subsistence allowance within a period of 60 days from the date of Judgment and order. 

 8. Mr. M.A Sobhan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner firstly submits that Bangladesh Agriculture Development Corporation, the petitioner is a statutory corporation, engaged in various functions as stated in the Ordinance of 1961, is neither a commercial establishment nor an industrial enterprises as such, the labour Court had no jurisdiction in entertaining the case under the I.R.O filed on behalf of the respondent No.2, as such, the judgment and order passed by the Labour Court in IRO Case No. 26 of 1994, is no legal effect. In support of his contention he relied on the case of Syedul Haque Bhuiyan Vs. Chairman BA DC 8 BLC (2003) 42 This decision was also upheld in the Appellate Division reported in 8 BLC (AD) (2003) 49, So far the merit of the case is concerned Mr. Sobhan, Advocate, submits that the respondent No.2, because of his misconducts was placed under suspension, by an order dated 2.6.1976 that the respondent No. 2 challenging his order of suspension filed a suit which was decreed as such the petitioner filed an appeal which was dismissed for default in 1981, that however, after the decree by an order dated 9.12.1978, he was transferred from his earlier placed of posting at Brahmanbaria to Chtndpur and was also released on 22.1.1979 but he did not join his new place of posting that besides, this order of transfer was also challenged in a writ petition being Writ petition No. 84 of 979 before the High Court Division and after hearing by its judgment dated 12.3.1991, the rule was discharged with costs. It is pointed out by Mr. Sobhan, Advocate that in the said judgment it is observed that after the decree passed by the Civil Court, since there was no order of stay, it would be deemed that petitioner was no long under suspension and as such he was obliged to join his new place of posting in accordance with the order passed by the concerned officials of the petitioner but the respondent No. 2 without complying with the orders of the authorities, remained without any trace for nearly 10 (Ten ) Years, as such, on his prayer being compassionate, the authorities by its order dated 23.1.1991 treated the said period as on duty without pay. In view of the above circumstance, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits, firstly the writ petition is not misconceived, secondly, the respondent No. 2 is not entitled to any arrear salary or emolument, as directed by the Labour Court. 

 10. We have heard the learned Advocates of both the parties and perused the application and the affidavits in opposition. It is admitted that by an order of 1976, the respondent No. 2, was placed under suspension, The said order of suspension was challenged in a suit being Title Suit No. 67 of 1976 in the Court of Munsif, Brahmanbaria After a contested the said suit was decreed by the Judgment and decree dated 21.7.1978 but the BADC filed an appeal being Title Appeal No. 232 of 1978 and by an Order dated 9.12.1978, transferred the respondent No. 2 from Brahmanbaria to Chandpur and released him from Brahmanbaria Zone by the memo dated 22.1.1979 but he did not comply with the said order, rather filed a writ petition being Writ petitioner No. 84 of 1979 . The Rule in the said Writ Petition was discharged with cost by the Judgment and Order dated 12.3.1981 (Annexure D-2), In the meantime, the appeal filed by the BADC was dismissed for default on 25.3.1981. As such, a miscellaneous case being Miscellaneous Case No. 11 of 1981 was filed praying for restoration of the appeal, the said miscellaneous case was rejected on contest by the Judgment and order dated 13. 7.1988. From the Office Order dated 23.1.1991 (Annexure-E), issued by the Executive Engineer (Irrigation). BADC, Brahmanbaria Region, it appears that a disciplinary proceeding was started against the respondent No. 2 by the memo no. 749/2(6) dated 11.4.1989 and in the due course an enquiry into the allegations against the respondent No. 2 was conducted. The enquiry officer by his enquiry report dated 24.10.1990 found him guilty in respect of the charge No.14 but other Charges were not proved. It also appears from the said Office order dated 23.1.1991 (Annexure-E) that by the memo no. 2006 dated 7.12.1988 his order of suspension v withdrawn but since he did not join his place of posting at Chandpur inspite of releasing him by the Order dated 22.1.1979, the period from 23.1.1979 to 11.5:1988 was treated as extra-ordinary have without pay, passed earlier by the order contained in Memo 82 dated 20.1.1990. Thus position was also maintained and re-affirmed by the Office Order dated 23.1.1991 (Annexure-F.1, The relevant portion of the said order is as follows: 

 11. Being aggrieved by the said order, the respondent No. 2 filed the IRO case. 

 12. Mr. M.A. Sobhan the learned Advocate, submits that the BADC is not a commercial establishment and since it is not a commercial establishment, its employees do not come within the definition of worker, as such, the IRO case, filed by the respondent No. 2 before the Labour Court, is not maintainable and the decision of the Labour Court in the said IRO case, is illegal being coram non Judice. In support of his contention the learned Advocate relies on the  decision in the case Syedul Haque Bhuiyan (Md.) Vs. Chairman BADC 8 BLC (2003) 42. 

 13. In that case, the petitioner, a store-Keeper of BADC, challenged his order dismissal. The objection as to the maintainability of the said writ petition was raised on the ground that the petitioner being, a worker, his remedy was before the Labour Court and not under Article 102 of the Constitution. On consideration of the relevant facts, the High Court Division found that the BADC cannot be termed as a commercial establishment or an industrial establishment (Pare-II of the Judgment). On appeal this view had also been accepted by the Appellate Division 8 BLC AD (2003) 49. 

 14. In view of the decision taken in both the Divisions of the Supreme Court, it is now established that the BADC is neither a commercial establishment not an industrial establishment, as such, the respondent No. 2 is not a worker and his IRO case filed before the Labour court was misconceived. 

 15. On the facts discussed above, it is found that the order of suspension dated 2.6.1976 was declared illegal in Title Suit No. 67 of: 1976; passed on 31.7.1978 but this was dragged on by the BADC till its Miscellaneous Case No 11 of 1981 was also rejected on 13.7.1988. Only thereafter by an order dated 7.12.1988 the order of suspension of the respondent No 2 was withdrawn and the period, of 2.6.1976 to 22.1.1979 was treated as his period of duty but since he did not join his new place of positing, the period from 23.1.1979 to 11.5.1988 was treated as extra ordinary leave without pay. We have examined the office order dated 9.12.1978 (Annexure-D) transferring the respondent No. 2 from Brahmanbaria to Chandpur and also the order dated 22.1.1979 (Annexure-D-1) releasing him from his office at Brahmanbaria. Both the letters referred to him as under suspension. Mr. Sobhan, Advocate, could not show any provision for transferring an employee during his suspension. 

 17. It is unfortunate that the authorities Of the BADC although placed him in suspension on 2.6.1976 but could neither draw any disciplinary proceeding against him nor withdraw its order of suspension. The order of suspension was finally withdrawn by the memo no 2006 dated 7.12.1988 after rejection of the miscellaneous case of BADC on. 13.7.1988 on that date on 7.12.1988, no disciplinary proceeding was pending against him. It is amazing that during this entire period the BADC could not start any disciplinary proceeding against him but fruitlessly kept him under suspension. 

 20. The respondent No. 2 successfully challenged this order in the IRO case No.34 of 1994 before the Labour Court but since the BADC is not a commercial establishment or an Industries establishment, he is not a worker and his IRO Case was misconceived. But such an objection with regard to the jurisdiction was not raised on behalf of the BADC before the Labour Court. As a matter of fact, the question of the lack of jurisdiction of the Labour Court was not even mentioned in the present writ petition Rather the BADC continued to claim itself as a commercial establishment before the High Court Division in the above noted case of Sayeedul Huq Bhuiyan (MD) and also canvassed it even before the Appellate Division but its petition for leave to appeal was rejected on 17.4.2002 on the finding that the BADC is not a commercial establishment. 

 22. It appears that the IRO case was filed in 1994 and the BADC contested the said case by filing a written statement and also examined as many as three witnesses but did not raise the question of jurisdiction of the labour court. In due course, the Labour-Court allowed the IRO case in part by its judgment and Order dated 26.5.2001 (Annexure-C) Being aggrieved, the BADC filed the present writ petition and although it was stated therein that in view of the facts and circumstances, its Judgment and Order was without jurisdiction but no specific ground on the lack of jurisdiction of the Labour Court was taken. As a matter of fact, the BADC itself not only accepted itself as a commercial establishment but also argued so in the case of Sayeedul Huq Bhuiyan up to the Appellate Division till it was decided otherwise in its judgment dated 17.4.2002 Only thereafter, the ground of lack of jurisdiction of the Labour Court was raised for the first time at the time of hearing of this writ petition, 10 (Ten) years after filing of IRO case in 1994. 

 23. As such the respondent No. 2 cannot really be blamed for filing the IRO case since the lack of Jurisdiction of the Labour Court was decided only in 2002 long after the disposal of the IRO case. BADC is also not responsible for this legal position, rather, it although canvassed in favour of jurisdiction of the Labour Court. 

 24. This is no doubt a very peculiar legal position. Be that as it may, we cannot presume or confer a jurisdiction upon the Labour Court which it does not process under the law, though it was so established at a very belated stage, still the judgment and order passed in IRO case was without jurisdiction. 

 28. In the instant case, the respondent no. 2 being aggrieved by the Order dated 23.1.1991 filed an IRO case on the legal position as was understood at that time in 1994 instead of filing a petition under Article 102, The legality of the said very Order dated 23.1.1991 was before the Labour Court for consideration. The BADC could not justify its said Order there. But although the respondent No. 2 got his relief but the Labour Court being without jurisdiction, its judgment and Order is of no legal effect. On the prayer of the BADC we have already hold so as prayed for. But since the respondent No 2 is not the petitioner, the question is whether we can further declare about the legality of the Order dated 23.1.1991 which was the sole question before the Labour Court. This question is important because this was not prayed for by the BADC, the petitioner, in this writ petition but it was prayed for on behalf of the respondent No.2 before the labour Court and this Writ Petition original from the said judgment and order of the Labour Court which considered the legality of the said Order. In effect the legality of the order dated 23.1.1991 passed by the BADC technically is still before this Court and cannot be bidden and shadowed by the mere fact that the present Rule was not issued at the instance of the respondent No. 2 but at the instance of the BADC whose order was under challenge at the instance of the actual aggrieved person, the respondent No. 2 in the IRO case. The jurisdiction of the Labour Court was raised only as a matter of procedures as a collateral question and that also admittedly at a much belated stage. 

 30. Let us try to perceive how in the case of Kendall V. Hamilton (1897) L.R. 4 AC 504, Lord Penzance pursuits the logic of Lord Mansfield in the case of Rice V Shute where there was an obvious error of procedure and Lord Mansfield said that he had consulted the other judges and that, 

 "It is clear, therefore, that, although the Defendant in such a case, may if he like, compel the plaintiff to discontinue his action and bring a fresh one against both, by means of a plea in abatement, there is yet a good cause of action against him which will sustain the verdict and judgment if the course be not followed." 

 31. Again on the question of technically, in the case of Kojo Pon V. Atta Fua AIR 1927 PC 264, Viscount Haldane dealt with a procedural error in this member at page-265: 

 "Their Lordships wish to say that   their first consideration always is to secure, if possible that substantial justice is done. That may not always be possible. These may be conditions in the local law or in the rules which preclude the possibility of getting round technical obstacles and doing complete justice. But they think that in the case of the rules of procedure in the Gold coast Colony there are no such obstacles. The Court was invested with the widest powers---- 

 32. Under these conditions their Lordships think that to refuse to hear the appeal merely on the ground of what might have been a mere technically about the bond was to fail to do justice as between the parties, and they are of opinion that the case must be remitted to the Court below the deal with it again, here it and, if necessary, get some formal proof of kwabena's authority but as at present advised their Lordships do not thin that necessary inasmuch as Kwabena's authority was accepted by the Registrar and inasmuch as he had acted right through and nobody till the other day ever challenged his authority." 

 33. These decisions were followed by Guha, J, in the case of Rahmani Bhuson Chowdhury V. Mohendra Kumar Shaha 6 DLR 156 where the suit was distnissed as a money suit but relief was granted in Second Appeal, holding it as a suit under the Bengal Money Lenders Aet, Guha, J. held at page-159, 

 36. Under the circumstances the Judgment and Order dated 26.42001 passed by the Second Labour Court, Dhaka in IRO Case No.26 of 1994 (Annexure-C) is declared to have been passed without lawful authority.
